summary: Describes an implementation strategy for BGP/MPLS IP VPNs where the outer tunnel label is replaced by an IP header or an IP header with GRE. This lets VPNs run over provider networks that do not support MPLS. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally these private networks travel on special label-switching roads. This explains how to use ordinary internet tunnels instead when the middle of the network does not offer those roads.

questions: how to run bgp mpls vpn without mpls core
subtitle: Tunnel VPN packets through networks without MPLS

tldr.problem: BGP/MPLS IP VPNs require MPLS Label Switched Paths between PE routers, but some provider networks do not support MPLS in their core.
tldr.mechanism: Replace the outermost tunnel MPLS label with either an IP or IP+GRE header that addresses the destination PE router directly, while keeping the VPN route label inside.
tldr.outcome: This enables BGP/MPLS VPN deployment over non-MPLS networks, as long as the PE routers themselves support MPLS and BGP.

today: RFC 4797 is an Informational RFC defining an implementation strategy for service providers to deploy BGP/MPLS VPNs over networks without MPLS in the core. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and remains relevant for hybrid network deployments.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A conventional BGP/MPLS IP VPN uses MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs) to carry traffic between Provider Edge (PE) routers across a service provider network. Each PE maintains Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instances to separate VPN traffic, and PE routers exchange reachability information using BGP. When an ingress PE receives a packet from a customer site, it assigns two labels: the innermost VPN route label identifies which VPN the packet belongs to, and the outermost tunnel label identifies the LSP to the egress PE.

This architecture works well when the entire provider network supports MPLS. However, when parts of the network cannot support MPLS, the VPN service cannot be deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: Private networks usually travel through special label-switching roads in a provider's network. This section explains how this system normally works, and why it fails when the middle of the network cannot handle labels.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
The core limitation of conventional BGP/MPLS IP VPNs is that they require an MPLS LSP connecting every ingress PE to every egress PE. If any router along this path does not support MPLS, the connection breaks and the VPN cannot be deployed.

This RFC describes a solution: instead of using an LSP as the tunnel between PE routers, use a regular IP tunnel or an IP tunnel wrapped in Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE). The PE routers themselves still understand MPLS and BGP/VPN concepts; the transit routers in between need only route standard IP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: If the routers in the middle of the provider network cannot handle labels, the regular VPN system breaks. This explains how to use a simpler tunnel that any router can handle.

sections.title: How MPLS-in-IP/GRE Works
sections.content:
The technical approach is straightforward: keep using MPLS labels to identify VPN routes, but wrap the MPLS packet in either an IP header or an IP+GRE header instead of tunneling it through an LSP.

When an ingress PE receives a packet from a customer, it looks up the destination IP address in the appropriate VRF to find the VPN-IP route. This lookup yields a VPN route label and the BGP Next Hop (the egress PE's address). The PE pushes the VPN route label onto the packet, then wraps it in MPLS-in-IP or MPLS-in-GRE encapsulation. The resulting packet has an IP header (or IP+GRE header) where the source address is the ingress PE and the destination is the egress PE. The transit routers forward this packet using ordinary IP routing, which requires no special MPLS capabilities.

The egress PE receives the IP-wrapped MPLS packet, removes the IP/GRE encapsulation to recover the MPLS packet, and switches it based on the VPN route label using standard MPLS forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a special label-switching tunnel, the ingress router wraps the labeled packet in a regular IP envelope addressed to the exit router. The middle routers just forward it like any other IP packet. The exit router unwraps it and delivers it using the label inside.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The encapsulation header's destination address is learned dynamically from the BGP Next Hop field of the MP_REACH_NLRI attribute. This means ingress PEs discover egress PE addresses automatically as VPN routes are distributed, with no need for manual tunnel configuration.

A critical requirement is that all PE routers in a network must have consistent tunnel capabilities. If some PEs use LSP tunnels while others use IP tunnels, each PE pair must be configured to use a common tunnel mechanism. The RFC notes that automatic association of tunnel capabilities on a per-peer basis is for future study.

Quality of Service (QoS) information from the VPN packet can be copied to the GRE/IP tunnel header to preserve forwarding behavior across the network. However, because GRE/IP tunnels lack traffic engineering capabilities, any traffic engineering features provided by the traditional LSP are lost.
sections.plainLanguage: The system automatically discovers which routers to tunnel to, but all routers in a provider network must agree on which tunneling method to use. The tunnel can carry quality-of-service information, but it cannot automatically choose the best path like MPLS can.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs and Spoofing
sections.content:
Replacing MPLS labels with IP encapsulation introduces security challenges. Traditional MPLS networks protect against spoofed packets by rejecting MPLS from outside the provider's boundaries. With IP encapsulation, spoofing protection requires filtering on every boundary router.

The provider can use either destination-based filtering (rejecting packets addressed to PE routers from outside) or source-based filtering (rejecting packets with internal source addresses from outside). If only source-based filtering is deployed, the RFC notes that the PE decapsulator should validate the IP source address of tunneled packets, though the RFC does not mandate this. Allocating tunnel IP addresses from a single IP block can simplify filter management.

The RFC references RFC 4023 (Encapsulating MPLS in IP or GRE) for detailed security guidance and requires service providers to apply those recommendations.
sections.plainLanguage: Using plain IP envelopes makes it easier for attackers to send fake packets to PEs. Providers must filter these at their network edges more carefully than they would with MPLS. Grouping the tunnel addresses in one IP block makes this filtering simpler.
